question: A small prairie system draws from a shallow dugout. Which seasonal change most directly increases the treatment challenge from algae growth?
correctAnswer: Longer daylight and warmer surface water in summer
explanation: Warm surface water with long daylight supports algae growth, which can raise turbidity, taste and odour, and filter loading.
options: Colder water and a thicker ice cover in January
Longer daylight and warmer surface water in summer
Lower wind speeds during calm autumn evenings
Higher groundwater levels after spring snowmelt
sourceTitle: US EPA - Small Drinking Water Systems Handbook
sourceReference: Supporting resource category: Source Water Assessment. See SOURCES.md: these are not claim-level verification citations.
optionA: Colder water and a thicker ice cover in January
optionB: Longer daylight and warmer surface water in summer
optionC: Lower wind speeds during calm autumn evenings
optionD: Higher groundwater levels after spring snowmelt

question: In rapid mix, alum is added to raw water. Which particle change does the alum produce first?
correctAnswer: It neutralizes particle charges so particles can clump
explanation: Alum first neutralizes the negative charges that keep fine particles apart, allowing them to come together in later flocculation.
options: It disinfects particles by destroying cell walls quickly
It grows large floc that settles within the rapid mix tank
It neutralizes particle charges so particles can clump
It raises particle size by filtering them through sand media
sourceTitle: WPI: 2025 Need-to-Know criteria
sourceReference: Supporting resource category: Coagulation Basics. See SOURCES.md: these are not claim-level verification citations.
optionA: It disinfects particles by destroying cell walls quickly
optionB: It grows large floc that settles within the rapid mix tank
optionC: It neutralizes particle charges so particles can clump
optionD: It raises particle size by filtering them through sand media

question: During gentle flocculation, paddle speed is increased sharply for several minutes. What happens to the floc that has already formed?
correctAnswer: It breaks apart into smaller pieces that settle poorly
explanation: Excess shear in flocculation breaks fragile floc into smaller fragments, which settle poorly and can pass to the filters.
options: It becomes denser and settles much faster than before
It stays the same size because shear has little effect
It breaks apart into smaller pieces that settle poorly
It dissolves back into the water as dissolved solids only
sourceTitle: WPI: 2025 Need-to-Know criteria
sourceReference: Supporting resource category: Flocculation Basics. See SOURCES.md: these are not claim-level verification citations.
optionA: It becomes denser and settles much faster than before
optionB: It stays the same size because shear has little effect
optionC: It breaks apart into smaller pieces that settle poorly
optionD: It dissolves back into the water as dissolved solids only

question: A clarifier receives flocculated water at a steady rate. Which condition in the basin allows floc to settle to the bottom instead of leaving with the clarified water?
correctAnswer: Water moves slowly enough for gravity settling to occur
explanation: Sedimentation depends on slow, even flow so gravity can pull floc down before water reaches the outlet weirs.
options: Water moves slowly enough for gravity settling to occur
Water moves quickly enough to keep all floc in suspension
Inlet jets stir the basin contents throughout the day
Outlet weirs draw water from the deepest part of the basin
sourceTitle: US EPA: Surface Water Treatment Rules — supporting treatment resources

optionA: Water moves slowly enough for gravity settling to occur
optionB: Water moves quickly enough to keep all floc in suspension
optionC: Inlet jets stir the basin contents throughout the day
optionD: Outlet weirs draw water from the deepest part of the basin

question: Water passes downward through a rapid sand filter after clarification. Which material is retained mainly within the upper part of the media bed early in a run?
correctAnswer: Fine floc and particles carried from the clarifier

question: An operator measures free chlorine residual after the contact tank. What does a measurable free residual at that point indicate?

The water contains no dissolved minerals or alkalinity
No chlorine was fed to the water during that shift at all
Chlorine remains available after demand has been exerted

question: A clear well level drops steadily during the morning peak while plant production stays constant. What does the drop tell the operator?
correctAnswer: Distribution demand is greater than plant production now
explanation: When outflow to distribution exceeds inflow from the plant, stored volume falls and the clear well level drops.
options: Distribution demand is lower than plant production now
Plant production has stopped completely during the peak
The clear well is gaining stored volume during the peak
Distribution demand is greater than plant production now

question: A raw water sample reads pH 6.2 and a treated sample reads pH 7.4. How do the two samples compare in acidity?

The treated sample is more acidic than the raw sample

Increase monitoring and adjust coagulant based on jar tests
Stop all raw water sampling until turbidity falls below 10 NTU
Add extra treated water storage by draining the clear well

Raise the feed toward the dose that formed good floc

Change the filter media before changing any chemical feed

question: Sludge has built up deeply in one corner of a rectangular clarifier and settled water quality is worsening on that side. What is the most direct corrective action?

Remove the accumulated sludge from that corner of the basin

Cover that corner so sunlight cannot reach the basin surface

question: A flocculation basin is 12 m long, 4 m wide and 2.5 m deep. Plant flow through the basin is 1800 m3/day. What is the detention time in the basin? Round to 1 decimal place.
correctAnswer: 1.6 hours
formula: Detention time (h) = Basin volume (m3) / Flow (m3/h); Volume = Length x Width x Depth; Flow (m3/h) = Daily flow / 24
explanation: Detention time = Volume / Flow. Substitution: volume = 12 x 4 x 2.5 = 120 m3, flow = 1800 / 24 = 75 m3/h, so 120 / 75 = 1.6 hours. Round to 1 decimal place.

tip: Check dimensional consistency and round only the final result.
options: 1.2 hours
